client: It's just...it's been six months since my mom passed, and I feel like I'm stuck in this dark place while everyone else has moved on. My friends keep inviting me out like normal, but when I go, I just feel so disconnected - like they don't understand how much it still hurts. Sometimes I wonder if therapy can even help with this kind of pain.
therapist: I hear how deeply painful this grief still feels for you, and how isolating it can be when others seem to have moved forward. The way your voice quickens when you describe feeling disconnected makes me wonder if there's some frustration or urgency beneath the sadness - like part of you wishes others could understand this pain more deeply.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
Yeah, it's exactly that. I feel like everyone expects me to be "over it" by now, but I'm not. Some days it hits me just as hard as the first week. My friends keep telling me to focus on the good memories, but that almost makes it worse because then I just realize those moments are gone forever. 

I don't know why I get so frustrated when people try to comfort me - part of me wants the support, but when they say things like "they'd want you to be happy," I just feel more alone. Like they don't really get how deep this pain goes.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between wanting comfort from others and feeling hurt when their words don't match the depth of your grief. I notice your voice lifts when talking about these interactions - almost like there's an extra layer of disappointment when well-meaning advice falls short of what you really need right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
Yeah, that's exactly it. I keep hoping someone will say the perfect thing that makes this pain feel less heavy, but then when they try, it just makes me feel more alone. Like they don't really get it, or they're just saying what they think they're supposed to say. 

Sometimes I even get angry at people for trying to help, which makes me feel guilty afterward. I know they mean well, but their "it'll get better with time" or "they're in a better place now" just makes me feel worse. Why does that happen? Shouldn't comforting words actually... comfort?
therapist:
It sounds like you're experiencing this deep conflict between wanting comfort and feeling hurt when it doesn't quite land right. I'm noticing that while you're describing these painful interactions, there's a sense of urgency in your voice - like you're really wrestling with why these well-meaning attempts at comfort aren't helping. 

What do you think would feel truly comforting to you right now, if you could create the perfect response from someone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know what would feel comforting anymore. That's part of the problem - when people try to help, it either feels fake or like they don't really get how bad I'm feeling. Sometimes I think I just want someone to sit with me in the mess instead of trying to fix it, but then I feel guilty for being so negative. 

It's like there's no right answer - if they try to cheer me up it feels dismissive, but if they agree it's bad then I just feel worse. I don't even know what I want from people anymore.
therapist:
What you're describing makes so much sense - the way your voice speeds up tells me how much this dilemma weighs on you. You're longing for connection but finding that most responses either feel too shallow or too heavy, and that exhausting back-and-forth is leaving you feeling even more alone. 

It might help to notice that you already have some wisdom here - when you mentioned just wanting someone to sit with you in the mess, that sounds like an important insight about what your grieving heart might truly need right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
Yeah, I guess that is what I need...but it's so hard to find people who can just sit with the mess without trying to fix it or run away. I feel like whenever I try to open up, people either give me clichés or get uncomfortable and change the subject. Then I just end up feeling worse for burdening them. 

I don't know how to ask for what I need without pushing people away. It's like I'm stuck between being too much and not being honest enough.
therapist:
Your voice carries such longing as you describe this struggle - wanting to share your pain but fearing it might be too much for others to hold. That rapid pace makes me wonder if part of you feels a sense of urgency to express this before the moment passes or before someone pulls away.

client:

It's like there's this crushing loneliness between wanting to be heard and knowing most people can't really handle deep emotions.
